title: Tondaraḍippoḍi Āzhwār
body:
The Chōḻa kingdom, rich in every kind of produce and watered by the Kāveri, was a land of great beauty and abundance, where lakes and streams wound through green fields. In this kingdom lay the village of Tirumaṇḍangudi, where the anthaṇars who lived there expounded the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma and Atharvaṇa Vedas. Among its people was a community known as the Kuḍumi Sōzhiya brāhmaṇas, also called the Vipras, whose daily life was devoted to the praise of Sriman Nārāyaṇa.

One of them, an anthaṇan named Veda Viśāradar, had great devotion to Emperumān and served Him by offering garlands every day. By the grace of Sriman Nārāyaṇa, in the year Prabhava, in the month of Mārgazhi, on Kṛshṇa Chaturthi, a Tuesday, under the Kēṭṭai nakshatram, a beautiful son was born to him as an amśam of the Vaijayanti, the garland of the Lord.

On the twelfth day after his birth, the child was named Vipra Nārāyaṇa. He was lovingly raised and given a sound education, together with devotion to Sriman Nārāyaṇa. He grew up with every good quality and a strong, well-formed body. For all his goodness, beauty and devotion, he was humble, and he treated elders and those younger than himself alike with respect.

One day, Sēnai Mudaliyār, the commander of the Lord's hosts, came down to earth and revealed to Vipra Nārāyaṇa why he had been born into this world and what he must do to attain mukti.

Learning the truth of his birth, he was filled with love and devotion for Sriman Nārāyaṇa, and he began to consider how best to express it. He resolved to worship at every kshethram where Emperumān gives His sevai, but wondered where to begin. After long thought, he decided to begin with the greatest of all the kshethrams of Sriman Nārāyaṇa, Srirangam, on the banks of the Kāveri, and he set out for it.

The Garden at Srirangam

Reaching the temple, he entered the sanctum and beheld Perumāl reclining upon Ādiśeshan. Overwhelmed by the beauty of Sri Ranganātha, he wished to see nothing else, and resolved that the rest of his life would be spent entirely in the service of Aranganāthan. Considering how to express his devotion, he decided to offer the Lord a garland every day.

So he laid out a great nandavanam, a flower garden, in Srirangam, planted with every kind of beautiful and fragrant flower, and built a small hut in its midst. Every morning he first offered his garland to Sri Ranganātha, and only then turned to the tasks of the day. Since he regarded Sri Ranganātha alone as the most beautiful thing in the world, he never turned his attention to any woman, and people came to think that he had no feelings for those around him.

Watching this from Sri Vaikuṇṭham, Tirumagaḷ, Sri Mahālakshmi, asked Sriman Nārāyaṇa how this man, so absorbed in devotion to Sri Ranganātha, could ever know how love is expressed, and what woman could ever win the heart of one like Vipra Nārāyaṇa. Knowing all that was to come, the Lord replied simply that she would soon see what would happen to him.

Dēvadēvi

In Tirukkarambanūr there lived two sisters, Dēvi, the elder, and Dēvadēvi, the younger, dancers who performed before kings. Both were so beautiful that they captivated all who saw them, and they were accomplished in both dance and song. In those days a Chōḻa king ruled from Uraiyūr, governing so well that the whole kingdom flourished in wealth and happiness. The king honoured Vedic scholars and musicians alike with generous gifts.

Hearing of this, Dēvi and Dēvadēvi resolved to display their art before the king and earn his reward. They went to the palace at Uraiyūr and danced and sang before him.

Delighted with their performance, the king showered them with costly gifts, diamonds and pearls. As they left Uraiyūr, Dēvadēvi suddenly wished to worship Sri Ranganātha, and the two sisters went to the temple at Srirangam.

On the way, they passed Vipra Nārāyaṇa's nandavanam, and its beauty and stillness drew them in. Dēvadēvi asked her sister whether they were on earth or in heaven, and who could have created so beautiful a garden.

Her sister replied that it belonged to Vipra Nārāyaṇa, a great devotee of Sriman Nārāyaṇa, who had made it so that he could offer garlands to the Lord every day.

Hearing this, Dēvadēvi wished to see him, and they went to his hut. Vipra Nārāyaṇa was watering the plants, and both sisters were struck by his beauty. Dēvadēvi fell in love with him at first sight and told him so, but he paid her no attention and went on with his work.

Seeing this, Dēvadēvi declared that she would win him over, and that she would stay there for a while. Her sister wished her well and left.

Dēvadēvi gave away all the gifts she had received from the king and put on simple saffron garments, such as ascetics wear. She went to Vipra Nārāyaṇa and told him that she had lived her life until then without being of use to anyone, a life no better than naragam, and that she wished to spend the rest of it with him in the service of Emperumān.

Vipra Nārāyaṇa was glad that another soul had come to serve the Lord, and being kind-hearted, he allowed her to stay and invited her in.

Days passed. One day it rained heavily. Vipra Nārāyaṇa was inside the hut, performing his daily pūjā to Sri Ranganātha. Dēvadēvi did not come inside but waited outside, and was drenched by the rain. So absorbed was he in his devotion that he did not notice what was happening outside.

When he finished his pūjā, he came out and saw Dēvadēvi soaked through. He asked her to come in and gave her his uttarīyam, his upper cloth, to dry herself.

Taking the cloth, she said that since he tended the garden and walked many miles each day to gather food, his legs must ache, and she asked whether she might massage them. He agreed. In such small ways she drew him towards her, until at last his heart turned completely, and they began to live together.

The Temple Vessel

One day Dēvadēvi told Vipra Nārāyaṇa that she wished to visit her mother and sister. He said that he would come with her, for he could not bear to be parted from her even for a moment, and they went together to her home.

There Vipra Nārāyaṇa gave everything he had to Dēvadēvi and her mother, until a day came when he had nothing left to give. Her mother then asked Dēvadēvi to send him away. Dēvadēvi, who truly loved him, could not bring herself to do it, but her mother would not have him in the house, and she told him to leave. Helpless, Vipra Nārāyaṇa left, wandered into a garden, and, utterly weary, fell asleep. Seeing this, Emperumān resolved to free him from māyā and set him on the path that leads to His sacred feet.

The Lord took the form of an ordinary man, went to Dēvadēvi's house and knocked at the door. Her mother asked who he was. He said that he was a disciple of Vipra Nārāyaṇa, and he handed her a large silver vessel, saying it was a gift from his guru for Dēvadēvi.

Receiving it, her mother thanked him and asked that his guru return to the house, for Dēvadēvi had been unwell ever since he left. The Lord, still in the guise of a disciple, went to Vipra Nārāyaṇa, woke him, and told him that Dēvadēvi's mother had asked him to return. Hearing this, Vipra Nārāyaṇa hurried back to the house and embraced Dēvadēvi.

The next morning the archaka entered the sanctum of Sri Ranganātha and found that a vessel used in the daily pūjā was missing. He reported it to the king, who sent his men to search for it, and they found it in Dēvadēvi's house.

They seized Dēvadēvi's mother and Vipra Nārāyaṇa and brought them before the king. When the king asked her mother where she had got the vessel, she said that a disciple of Vipra Nārāyaṇa had given it to her. But Vipra Nārāyaṇa denied this, saying that he had no disciple. After consulting the elders of the court, the king ordered that Vipra Nārāyaṇa be held in prison for the night, and Dēvadēvi's mother was set free.

That night, Vipra Nārāyaṇa wept and asked Emperumān why this had befallen him, and he prayed. The same night, Emperumān appeared in the king's dream, told him all that had happened, and asked him to set Vipra Nārāyaṇa free.

The next day, Vipra Nārāyaṇa was honoured in the court as a devotee of Sriman Nārāyaṇa should be, and was given many precious gifts. The king explained that all of it had been a tiruviḷaiyāḍal, a divine play of Emperumān.

The Dust of the Devotees' Feet

Now knowing truly why he had come into the world, he went to the temple of Sri Ranganātha and sang the Lord's praise. He bowed before the devotees of Sriman Nārāyaṇa, placed upon his head the dust from beneath their feet, and sang in praise of Sri Ranganātha.

From then on he was called Tondaraḍippoḍi Āzhwār, "the Āzhwār who is the dust of the feet of the Lord's devotees." Having at last realised the purpose of his birth, he went on to worship at the kshethrams of Sriman Nārāyaṇa and sang the Lord's praise.
